one_liner: AVX2 patch to the HQC Round-2 KEM's sparse-dense multiply and BCH syndrome step; 34-46% fewer cycles than the optimized reference.
what_it_does: This is a 2019 research patch (Bessonov, Robert and Véron) for the NIST Round-2 HQC optimized implementation, a code-based post-quantum KEM. It replaces two profiled hotspots: sparse_dense_mul, which multiplies a low-weight secret or error vector by a dense polynomial mod X^N-1, and the BCH decoder's syndrome_gen. The crypto_kem_keypair/enc/dec API is unchanged and, per the report, the output is KAT-identical; the patch is applied at compile time by #including patch.c and patch2.c into hqc.c and bch.c under PATCH/PATCH2 macros. Only hqc-256-3 is packaged as a ready tree; the other parameter sets exist only in per-table experiment folders under Arith2020.
how_it_is_fast: The 'fast convolution' keeps the sparse operand as a list of its w nonzero positions (67-153), so the product is the XOR of w copies of the dense polynomial, each shifted by one of those positions. Each shift is done with AVX2 256-bit shifts (_mm256_slli/srli_epi64 plus a carry from the neighboring word) and XORed into a double-length accumulator, followed by one vectorized reduction mod X^N-1; the baseline instead used an NTL-inspired vectorized multiply. syndrome_gen2 spreads the received BCH codeword bits into bytes with a shuffle and mask, then XOR-accumulates rows of a precomputed alpha^(ij) table, 16 syndromes per ymm register, instead of evaluating each syndrome separately in GF(2^10).
when_to_use: Studying or reproducing HQC Round-2 performance on x86-64 with AVX2 (Haswell and later): keygen, encapsulation and decapsulation for N = 24,677-70,853.

As a reference technique for multiplying a sparse position list by a dense polynomial in F2[X]/(X^N-1), in quasi-cyclic code-based schemes where the sparse operand has weight around 100 and N is tens of thousands of bits. The report puts the multiplication alone at about 64-75% faster.
As a template for vectorized BCH syndrome computation with a precomputed power table (400,209 to 18,101 cycles, about 22x, for n1 = 766 in the report).
when_not_to_use: Anything deployed. The code is not constant-time: fastConvolutionMult indexes memory by the secret sparse positions (C256[vbi], tab[i64]), and syndrome_gen2 branches on bits of the decoded word.

Current HQC. This targets the Round-2 code base and its six parameter sets (hqc-128-1 ... hqc-256-3). liboqs now ships HQC-1/3/5 from the official 20250822-spec implementation (re-enabled by default in 0.16.0, July 2026), so the percentages and code will not carry over as-is.
Multi-threaded use. Scratch buffers (C2, TT, tmp8), syndrome_gen2's static tmp_array and the precomputed tables are process-global mutable state.
Any use that needs a license. The repo has no LICENSE file and has been abandoned since April 2020 (6 stars, no issues, no releases).
Non-x86 or pre-AVX2 CPUs; the Arith2020 experiments additionally need PCLMUL and, for several tables, the gf2x 1.2 library.

integration.form: source-drop (compile-time patch over the HQC Round-2 optimized source tree)
integration.dependencies: OpenSSL libcrypto (SHA-512 wrapper; the NIST rng/seedexpander in lib/), make, gcc; gf2x 1.2 for the Arith2020 TABLE1/2/3/5 experiments
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 required (the Arith2020 folders also need PCLMUL); benchmarked on Intel Core i5-4690S and i5-8400H, the latter with gcc 7.4.0 on Ubuntu 18.04
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: file-scope global scratch buffers in patch.c, a static buffer in syndrome_gen2, and global GF/alpha tables that must be initialized once by calling syndrome_gen_init() from main.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — keeps the NIST crypto_kem_* API and KAT-identical output for the Round-2 hqc-256-3 code, but only as a patch to that obsolete code base, not to any current HQC implementation

gotchas: The PATCH2 syndrome path reads global tables that syndrome_gen_init() must fill first. Forgetting that call leaves them NULL. The init also prints to stdout and never frees its roughly 200 KB alpha^(ij) table (796 x 128 int16 for hqc-256-3).
Patches are switched on by rewriting src/patch.h, which script.sh overwrites with '#define PATCH' between builds. Building by hand gives whatever the header currently says.

The randomized FastConvolution variant (Arith2020 Rand_FC) shuffles the order of the sparse positions using libc rand(), which is not a cryptographic RNG, and it keeps the same position-indexed accumulator writes (C256[vbi]).
The report's 'speed-up %' is a reduction in cycles. 34-46% fewer cycles is about 1.45-1.86x in speed ratio, and the 70-75% figure applies to the multiplication kernel only, not the whole KEM.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only key-encapsulation and code-based post-quantum entry in this category. ENG25519 and UltrafastSecp256k1 are classical elliptic-curve code and VecFalcon is a post-quantum signature. Pick it only to study HQC or quasi-cyclic binary-polynomial arithmetic on AVX2; it is not a deployable alternative to any of them.
verified_claims_summary: Against the HQC Round-2 optimized implementation on a 4th-gen Core i5-4690S (Turbo off, compiler not stated), both patches together cut keygen cycles 34.9-42.8%, encapsulation 33.7-45.2% and decapsulation 45.0-46.3% across all six parameter sets. On an i5-8400H with gcc 7.4.0 (-O3 -mavx2) the reductions were 30.9-43.2%, about 1.45-1.86x in speed. Each figure is the mean of per-dataset minimum cycle counts over 1,000 runs for 50 random data sets.
status_note: Abandoned since April 2020 and unlicensed, and it patches a superseded Round-2 HQC code base with non-constant-time kernels. Read it for the technique; do not vendor it. The authors' later constant-time Karatsuba/Toom-Cook multiplication work (Robert & Véron, J. Cryptographic Engineering 2022) is the more relevant follow-up.
